verdicts.explanation: The Livac t-LBO value σion = 7.0 × 10−5 S cm−1 is stated in Section 3.1 right after the Ref. [26] discussion of Li-vacancy transport, and this paper does not compute ionic conductivity itself. Literature_cited is the closest origin, though the sentence lacks an explicit citation marker.

Section 3.2 says 'we recall its Li-ion transport properties from Ref. [26]: its ionic conductivity is σion = 7.0 × 10−13 S cm−1', matching the material, value, unit, and literature_cited origin; no temperature is given.

The paper states 'as reported in our previous work [26], ... the Bvac m-LBO possesses the highest Li-ionic conductivity (σion = 2.8 × 10−2 S cm−1)', so the value, material and literature_cited origin are right, and no temperature is stated.
Section 3.2 says 'our previous work reported that the Ovac m-LBO ... σion = 6.1 × 10−6 S cm−1 (Ref. [26])', matching the value, material and literature_cited origin; no temperature is stated.

Section 3.1 says 'our previous work (see Ref. [26]) showed that the ionic conductivity of the Ovac t-LBO is estimated to be σion = 7.6 × 10−8 S cm−1', matching the value, material and literature_cited origin; no temperature is stated.

The Introduction attributes the total conductivity 'ca. 10−6 S cm−1' for t-LBO to Hirose et al. [24], measured by EIS between 450 and 520 K on high-pressure-synthesized samples, so the value, kind, temperature, method and literature_cited origin all check out.
